what: Avis Budget Group rents cars through the Avis, Budget and Zipcar brands at airports and neighbourhood locations around the world, and owns a fleet of several hundred thousand vehicles.
customers: Business and leisure travellers, and people who need short-term car access through Zipcar.
money: Car rental in the US, Canada and Latin America.
Car rental in Europe, Asia-Pacific and other markets.
moat: Strong brands, airport locations and scale in fleet buying and financing.
risks: Shareholders’ equity is deeply negative ($-3.2B) after years of buybacks and losses.
Losses of $1.8B in 2024 and $889M in 2025, mostly from writing down the value of its fleet as used car prices fell.
Debt of $9.3B, plus fleet financing that makes the balance sheet fragile.
Used car prices and rental demand both swing with the economy.
opportunities: Revenue held steady at about $11.6–12B a year.
Operating cash flow of $2.7B over the last twelve months.
Fleet costs per car should fall as the fleet is refreshed at lower prices.
Share count fell from 66M in 2021 to 35M in 2025.
watch: Fleet cost per unit per month and rental pricing.
view: Avis is a highly leveraged bet on rental pricing and used-car values. It made huge profits in 2021–2023 when cars were scarce and used them to buy back half its shares; since then, falling used-car prices forced large write-downs of its fleet and two years of losses.
Equity is now deeply negative and debt is large, so the shares behave like an option on recovery. If fleet costs fall and pricing holds, earnings can rebound quickly; if not, the leverage hurts.

This turns on fleet costs and used-car prices. I would call it a speculative, leveraged position rather than a value investment, suitable only for investors who can stomach large swings in both directions.
bull: Fleet costs fall, pricing holds and earnings rebound strongly on a shrunken share count.
bear: A recession hits travel demand and used-car prices, squeezing a stretched balance sheet.
